lede.text: Dabu is a mud-resist hand block printing technique, named from the Hindi word dabana, to press, in which a paste of clay, lime and gum keeps dye from the parts of the cloth it covers.

Kaur calls it the most popular and favoured printing of Rajasthan and names Bagru, Barmer, Kaladera, Jodhpur and Akola near Chittorgarh as its centres, and Impart also describes dabu printing at Balotra.

Kaur wrote in 2011 that Chhipa printers make it with vegetable dyes for communities such as the Jat, Mali and Rabari, though Impart noted in 2022 that natural indigo, yellow and red have given way to synthetic products such as Naphthol.
Impart traces dabu's origins as far back as the eighth century, from a fabric specimen found in Central Asia, though sources differ on where it originated.

sentences.text: Impart traces dabu's origins as far back as the eighth century, from a fabric specimen found in Central Asia.
Kaur holds, while noting that little physical proof survives, that dabu was developed centuries before the Mughals invaded India and is originally Indian.
Sources differ on its origin: Apparel magazine's 2019 feature says it originated in the tribal regions of Rajasthan, and Impart traces its roots in India to the village Akora.
Kaur writes that printing in Rajasthan was patronised by royals, while the many centres without royal patronage practised the folk form of printing called dabu.
She notes that medieval literature has the words uchcho, for the print industry, and champai, for the chippa or printer.

Kaur writes that dabu almost lost its relevance with modern printing as a time-consuming process with less profit, and that while many chippas opted for new trends in art and craft, some tried to keep it alive for modern buyers with support from the Government of Rajasthan.
Impart noted in 2022 that naturally derived indigo, yellow and red have given way to synthetic products such as Naphthol, and that tar has come to be used instead of the mud resist.
At Bagru women have traditionally done dabu printing, though Raj and Choudhuri note that men are also taking it up.
Kaur's dabu process begins by washing and desizing the cloth, treating it with harda and printing syahi and begar pastes, though the sequence of stages varies with the pattern wanted.
After the design is block printed, the dabu is printed, mostly with the data block, or spread with a brush where the original background colour must not be disturbed.
Sawdust sprinkled on the wet paste absorbs water and gives additional layers of resist, and the cloth is left in the sun to dry before the indigo tanks.
In Kaur's account the cloth is soaked in a nine feet deep maat for 15 to 20 minutes, aired by two people and soaked again, half a dozen times.
Applying more resist between indigo dips keeps chosen areas at the shade already reached, giving a range of blue shades.
In the Bagru GI journal's process the resist is removed by soaking the cloth for at least 3 to 4 hours and beating it on a flat stone slab, while Kaur describes rinsing it in flowing water.
Because cloth must dry properly before more dabu is applied, dabu work is not done in the rainy season.
Dabu paste is made of kali mitti or black clay, lime, gum and beedan, though sources differ on whether beedan is moth-eaten wheat flour, pounded wheat chaff or a natural gum.
Kaur explains that the lime thickens the solution, the clay holds the ingredients together and the gum helps wash the resist away after the final dyeing.
Kalidar, dolidar and gwar wali dabu are the most popular kinds in Rajasthan; dolidar has more gum and withstands about two trips to the dye vats, and gawarbali adds oil and gawar seed powder.

Three strengths of resist are used: lime for fine outlines, clay for cloth dipped in indigo a few times, and sand for very absorbent pomegranate and ferrous dyes, though the Bagru GI journal says the dhabu technique is used only for indigo patterns.
Mein ki dabu, a wax resist, was made by heating honeybee wax, chir pine solution, tilli oil and ghee, and taking it off the cloth with soda ash in hot water is called ukala.
The art of making dabu paste is kept secret, and each printing family follows its own recipe.
Impart wrote in 2022 that dabu, once used in costlier textiles such as Maheshwari cotton, is now used on silk, crepe and georgette.
Kaur names Bagru near Jaipur, Barmer, Kaladera, Jodhpur and Akola near Chittorgarh as dabu centres, and writes that dabu was popular wherever Rajasthan had an abundance of water.
Akola is described as a village of Chittorgarh district, though Asia InCH and Gaatha describe it as a craft cluster in Udaipur district.
The Bagru GI journal places Bagru and Kaladera in Jaipur district, while Kaur puts Kaladera near Udaipur.
Impart in 2022 described Balotra, then a city in Barmer district, as a centre where cloth is first direct printed with wooden blocks and then dabu printed.
Balotra was among the new districts Rajasthan approved in 2023, and Scroll reports that the state government decided to retain it.
One of two Piparcity artisans who make Fabindia's Indigo Collection at a manufacturing location in Jodhpur told IANS in 2018 that it is naturally dyed using dabu, Bagru and ajrakh.
Traditionally dabu is used to keep either the printed part or the background portion of the cloth white.
Kaur describes tor datai, podh datai and rata datai, styles that put dabu on the syahi outline, on parts of the design such as leaves or stems, or on designs already coloured with syahi or begar.
Dabu blocks are carved with motifs such as peacocks, mangoes, leaves, corn stalks and sunflowers, and with lines, dots and chevrons, and the patterns are handed down over generations.
Kaur writes that each motif is tied to a specific community and identifies the wearer's community.
Dabu print was widely known on women's ghagras and was also used on the fetiya skirt and the bandhej lugda, though one feature says it was once used exclusively on cotton saris.
Modern dabu designs add geometric waves, graphic elements and shapes, and use more colour combinations of red, green and black.
Aavaran in Udaipur has contributed to the revival and promotion of dabu, and IANS reports that Fabindia and Aavaran gave the dabu print industry more visibility and a more diverse buyer base.
Besides garments, dabu is often used in accessories, furnishings and home decoration.
IANS describes dabu as one of the most labour-intensive printing works, which raises prices, and reports that powerloom makes its designs easier to replicate and steal.
Apparel magazine's 2019 feature says dabu is labour intensive, few artists can do it justice, and its natural dyes and vegetable pastes are costly and hard to find.
Indigo has poor affinity for the cloth in the presence of water, so the first dip gives a pale sky blue and darker blue needs repeated dips and oxidation.
Exposed to air, the reduced indigo oxidises to its insoluble blue form, which adheres to the fibres.
In the Bagru GI journal's process, a vat ready for use is kept alive by constant additions of indigo, lime and jaggery.
Dyeing with alizarin develops a rich red colour where begar, a mordant of alum, iron oxide and local tree gum, was printed.
In the Bagru GI journal's process, alum fixing of the yellow dye lasts only a few minutes, because a long soak makes the dhabu come off.
